The "CAPE ASPY" departed Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, on 30 January 1993, bound for the Georges Bank fishing g rounds. Approximately 14 hours later, while still en route, the vessel sank in rough weather conditions, in 120 fathoms, in position 42°28.6'N, 65°y58.2'W, with the loss of five lives.The Board determined that the "CAPE ASPY" proceeded to sea in rough weather conditions with many weathertight/watertight openings to the hull either in the open or in the closed but unsecured condition. The combined effects of rough weather, sea spray ice accretion, free surface effect of shipped seas retained on deck, in conjunction with the vessel's low transverse stability and the downflooding to the hull, caused the "CAPE ASPY" to lose all reserve buoyancy and sink.

On 17 December 1990, the F.V. "STRAITS PRIDE II", inbound to St. John's, Newfoundland, from the fishing grounds with a two-third load of round (ungutted) codfish stowed in the fish hold, encountered adverse weather, capsized and sank throwing the six-person crew into the ice-cold waters. Three crew members who managed to board the inflatable liferaft were subsequently rescued, but the remaining three lost their lives.The Transportation Safety Board of Canada determined that the vessel continued to fish after learning of a forecasted storm warning and that the combined effects of the weather, shipped seas, stowage of the catch, free surface effect of liquids, loss of the port paravane, and downflooding caused the vessel to capsize and sink by the stern. The suddenness of the capsizing precluded efforts by three of the crew to successfully abandon the vessel, displacing them into the sea. As they were wearing only normal winter clothing with approved lifejackets, their survival time was limited. The other three crew members boarded the liferaft from the sea and were rescued some eight hours later in a mildly hypothermic condition.

On 16 December 1990, while returning in heavy weather from fishing grounds in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the "NADINE", a 37-metre fishing vessel, listed to port and sank by the stern. A search and rescue operation was immediately undertaken to locate the ten people aboard. Two crew members were rescued and the bodies of six victims were recovered. Two crew members are still missing.The Board determined that the "NADINE" sank because the openings on the afterdeck and in the transverse bulkheads were not secured. Water was thus able to enter the vessel and eventually flood the lazaret, the fish holds and the engine-room. This ingress gradually reduced the vessel's stability until all reserve buoyancy was lost and the vessel sank. Poor weather, darkness, lack of training and the suddenness of the sinking hindered the abandonment and contributed to the loss of life.

The following accident occurred on July 16, 2010, at approximately 1521 hours.  The operator of Vessel I was towing two children on a tube behind the vessel.  He realized that he needed to refuel the vessel and headed toward shore. He passed to the right of a swim raft that was about 200 feet from shore and to the left of a moored boat (Vessel II).  As he swung the vessel parallel to the shoreline, the tube "whipped" out behind Vessel I and collided with the bow of Vessel II.  The operator claimed that he had cut power to the vessel as he passed the boat and was not under power as he turned into the beach; however, witnesses all estimated the Vessel's I's speed to be too fast for an area where there were so many obstacles around.  As the tube approached Vessel II, one of the tubers (Victim II) either jumped off or fell out of the tube just before colliding with Vessel II.  The other tuber (Victim I) was protected from striking Vessel II due to the tube flipping up between him and the boat.  Victim II was unconscious and floating in the water after his impact with Vessel II.  Both victims were brought to shore and transported to the hospital by EMS.  Victim I suffered a bump on the head and minor whiplash.  Victim II suffered a fractured skull and bleeding of the brain.  He was in a coma for approximately two weeks following the accident.  After coming out of the coma, he began speech and occupational therapy.
